one_line: Kai Explains argues the viral DeepSeek margin math misses the point: DeepSeek's economics come from KV-cache hit rates, not raw GPU throughput, and the cache layer is the part left closed.
summary: The video dissects DeepSeek's late-October 2026 releases (V4.1 Flash 1017, the DeepInfer inference engine, a search API) and the viral claim that DeepSeek earns very high margins per GPU. The naive math (155T tokens/day at $38 per GPU-hour) implies about $22.7B/year, roughly 23x DeepSeek's reported ~$1B run rate, so most tokens must be served from a KV cache rather than computed. The reported cache hit rate rose from 56.3% (Feb 2025) to 96%, cutting compute per input token about 11x, and a cache hit costs about 50x less than a miss. The speaker argues the open-sourced DeepInfer covers the compute path while the distributed cache, prefill/decode split and load balancing stayed internal, and that the released engine is no faster than vLLM on the same benchmark. For buyers, identical open-weight price sheets across hosts hide large differences in effective cost via hit rate, cache retention window and whether a cache survives a change of replica. Several cross-checks are back-of-envelope figures built on third-party numbers (SemiAnalysis, The Information) that the speaker did not verify.
speakers: Kai (channel host, name not given in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: The headline margin math is misread: 155T tokens/day at $38 per GPU-hour implies about $22.7B/yr, about 23x DeepSeek's ~$1B run rate, so most tokens are not computed fresh.
key_ideas.detail: Naive estimate needs ~68,000 GPUs at a 26,300 tok/s peak per GPU; the $1B run rate implies ~3,000 GPUs. The gap is explained by cache reuse.

key_ideas.idea: The KV cache is the core economic lever: a stored prefix is loaded instead of recomputed, and a cache hit is about 50x cheaper than a miss at the quoted off-peak prices.
key_ideas.detail: Multi-turn agent sessions resend the whole history each turn; an identical prefix (e.g. first 79k of 80k tokens at turn 40) can be served from cache.

key_ideas.idea: Cache hit rate rose from 56.3% (Feb 2025 paper) to 96% (DeepInfer release), which the speaker reads as ~11x less compute per input token on the same chips.
key_ideas.detail: Per-token KV footprint reportedly fell to 890 bytes, about a quarter of the prior Flash model, letting more context fit on SSD tiers (~100 PiB cited).

key_ideas.idea: Revenue decomposes around the cache: per 100 tokens served, ~95 are cache reads, ~4 computed input, ~1 output; by the quoted prices the output token brings in ~41% of revenue, cached reads ~19%.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says the single output token pays as much as all 95 cached reads; by his own prices it is closer to 2x. The $38/GPU-hour figure is therefore better read as a cache number.

key_ideas.idea: The open release is narrower than the headline: model weights (MIT), DeepInfer engine (Apache 2.0), GPU kernels, a Rust request library and the 3FS file system are open; the KV cache system, prefill/decode split and load balancing are not.
key_ideas.detail: The README lists those three missing pieces as required for a complete service; the speaker links it to DeepSeek's April 2025 argument that its engine was tightly coupled to internal infrastructure.

key_ideas.idea: The released engine is not a speed advantage: it supports only offline, single-turn inference per SemiAnalysis, and vLLM reportedly matches its published benchmark numbers.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker reads the recipe library as a distribution strategy: good third-party hosts of the weights are marketing for DeepSeek.

key_ideas.idea: Identical list prices hide a large cost spread driven by hit rate: the same price sheet yields about 1.8c, 6.5c and 13.5c per 1M input tokens at 96%, 80% and 56.3% hit rates.
key_ideas.detail: Providers differ in cache retention (days vs. paid 5-minute or 1-hour guarantees vs. best effort) and whether the cache is replica-local (Fireworks) or on shared storage (DeepSeek).

key_ideas.idea: Self-hosting this stack is a data-center project: minimum 128 GPUs (64 prefill + 64 decode) on Blackwell or Ascend 950, roughly 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU for cache, and the hard part (cache lookup across machines) is not in the repo.
key_ideas.detail: Full weights 510 GB; smallest community build cited at 233 GB; the 4-bit build is 501 GB because export layers already ship in 4-bit.

key_ideas.idea: Use cases where this analysis does not apply: US federal civilian use under the DHS order, data that cannot go to a China-operated API, and long agentic builds where per-step accuracy dominates cost.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker cites ProgramBench 37.0 vs 29.1 and TerminalBench 4.0 51.8 vs 42.3 in favour of Claude Opus 5 (his figures, not verified), and notes a US-hosted host (DeepInfra) with zero data retention.

key_ideas.idea: The buyer's first question should be how long a provider keeps your cache and whether a hit survives landing on a different machine, not price per million tokens.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker's closing checklist framing for agent and long-context workloads.

techniques.name: Effective input cost from hit rate
techniques.how: Cost per 1M input tokens = hit_rate x hit_price + (1 - hit_rate) x miss_price. Read cached vs. uncached token counts from each response (DeepSeek reports them) and back out the blended rate. Example with $0.30 miss and $0.006 hit: 96% -> ~1.8c, 80% -> ~6.5c, 56.3% -> ~13.5c per 1M input.
techniques.when: Comparing hosts of the same open-weight model, or estimating an agent session's real cost from an invoice.

techniques.name: Keep a stable prompt prefix across turns
techniques.how: The cache only helps when the leading tokens are byte-identical to a stored prefix, so new content should be appended at the end rather than inserted or reordered earlier. (Implied by the speaker's turn-39 vs. turn-40 example; he does not give explicit prompt-engineering rules.)
techniques.when: Long multi-turn agent sessions where history is resent every turn.

techniques.name: Sticky routing for replica-local caches
techniques.how: If a provider's cache lives on one replica (speaker cites Fireworks), requests must keep landing on the same machine or hits are lost. Route by session or prefix hash, or prefer providers with shared cache storage.
techniques.when: Self-run or multi-replica gateways serving open-weight models.

techniques.name: Provider checklist for caching
techniques.how: Ask: how long is the cache retained (days vs. minutes vs. guaranteed tiers, and whether guarantees cost extra)? Does a hit survive a different machine? Is the cache charged at a separate rate? Is data retained or stored in a US region?
techniques.when: Choosing an inference host for agent or long-context workloads.

techniques.name: Back-of-envelope check on vendor throughput claims
techniques.how: tokens/day / 86,400 = tokens/s; divide by per-GPU throughput (at stated concurrency) to get GPU count; multiply by rental rate for implied revenue; compare with reported revenue. A large mismatch implies cache reuse or other hidden work.
techniques.when: Evaluating claims about serving margins or cluster size before trusting them.

tools: DeepSeek KV cache technical report 'Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression'

numbers.claim: V4.1 Flash: 552B total params, ~16B active per output token, ~8B per input token; 1M-token context; MIT weights; DeepSWE 74.2 -> 77.0
DeepSeek search API priced at $0.75 per 1,000 requests; free built-in search ends Nov 1
155T tokens/day per cluster at $38 per GPU-hour; B300 rental $3 (long-term) to $18 (on demand); SemiAnalysis ~$50/hr profit at 60% utilization; ~$1B/yr revenue (reported)
Peak 26,300 tok/s per GPU at 256 concurrent requests; ~68,000 GPUs needed for 155T/day; implied $22.7B/yr vs ~$1B actual (23x gap); ~3,000 GPUs implied
Off-peak prices: cache hit ~0.3c vs miss ~15c per 1M tokens (~50x); output ~200x a cache hit
Cache hit rate 56.3% (Feb 2025) -> 96% (DeepInfer release): ~11x less compute per input token
KV footprint 890 bytes/token (~1/4 of prior Flash); ~100 PiB SSD cache; ~127T tokens of capacity
Cache retention: 3 days for agent conversations, 7 days for chatbot conversations
Per 100 tokens served: ~95 cache reads, ~4 computed input, ~1 output; revenue share ~19% / ~40% / ~41%
Peak sheet on OpenRouter: ~40 providers; $0.30/M input, $1.20/M output, $0.006/M cache hit
Blended input price per 1M at same list price: 96% hit ~1.8c, 80% ~6.5c, 56.3% ~13.5c (~7.6x spread)
Invoice example: 89.5M tokens billed for $0.54 (mostly hits) vs ~$13.42 if billed as misses
Self-host minimum 128 GPUs (64 prefill + 64 decode); full weights 510 GB; smallest community build 233 GB; 4-bit build 501 GB
Cache SSD budget ~14.4 TB per GPU
Claude Opus 5 vs V4.1 Flash (speaker's figures): ProgramBench 37.0 vs 29.1; TerminalBench 4.0 51.8 vs 42.3; DeepInfra 51% price cut on Oct 17

hot_takes: The 'profitable at 80% margins' headline misreads the economics: the $38/GPU-hour figure is mostly a cache number, not a GPU number.
'Open-sourced their entire inference stack' overstates the release; the cache system, prefill/decode split and load balancing stayed internal.
The claim that the one output token pays as much as all 95 cached reads is overstated: by the speaker's own prices (~$1.20/M output vs ~$0.006/M hit x 95 tokens) it is roughly 2x.

The invoice comparison mixes prices: $0.54 matches the ~0.6c hit price, but $13.42 matches the off-peak ~15c miss price, not the peak $0.30 miss price. The true gap on one sheet is ~50x per token, not the quoted figure.

Several key numbers (revenue, margins, GPU count, Claude Opus 5 benchmark scores, SemiAnalysis and The Information figures) come from third parties or the speaker's own arithmetic and were not independently checked in the video.
Caption-level name errors are likely (e.g. 'Paracel' for Parasail, 'Onslaught' for a community build, 'cash' for 'cache'); names here are corrected where obvious.

relevance.why: InferCraft already plans pluggable KV-cache strategies (H2O, CPU offload, LMCache). The talk's cache-hit sensitivity and retention/replica-locality framing is directly relevant to how InferCraft should be evaluated.
relevance.action: Add cache-hit and cache-miss token accounting to InferCraft's KV-cache strategy benchmarks, and report effective $/M input at 56%, 80% and 96% hit rates, as the talk's sensitivity table does.

relevance.why: Long resumed Claude Code runs resend large histories each turn, so cache behaviour determines their real cost. The talk is about DeepSeek, not Claude, so the transfer is indirect.
relevance.action: Record cache-read vs. uncached input tokens per checkpointed run to see what long or resumed sessions actually cost before optimising them.
